text: Watch a speedrunner finish a game that takes most players twenty hours in under fifteen minutes, and you'd swear they must have lightning-fast fingers. text: Most people walk straight past sea cucumbers. They look like soggy sausages lying on the sand, and they hardly move. They come in many colours, from plain brown to bright orange with blue spots. But without these lumpy creatures, coral reefs would be in serious trouble. A sea cucumber spends its day swallowing sand and digesting the tiny scraps of dead plants and animals in it. Then it poos out clean sand behind it. A single sea cucumber can clean dozens of kilograms of sand every year. Its droppings also release nutrients that help nearby coral and seagrass grow. Without them, waste would pile up on the sea floor, and the coral would struggle to grow. Sea cucumbers have some revolting habits, too. Many breathe through their bottoms. Some shoot out their own sticky guts to tangle attackers, then grow new ones. A small fish called a pearlfish sometimes lives inside a sea cucumber's bottom and pops out at night to feed. In some places, so many sea cucumbers have been collected that the sand around reefs has turned smelly and murky. Marine scientists are now working to protect them, because a reef with no sea cucumbers is like a city where nobody takes out the rubbish.
